attack: Concurrent nonce race — 2 parallel requests carrying one authorisation, compliant facilitator
expectation: Releases equals settled transactions equals one, however many requests arrive in parallel.
observed: 2 parallel accesses on one decision against the durable PostgreSQL store: 1 released, 1 settlement calls. Refusal reasons: NONCE_ALREADY_CONSUMED.
notes: Atomic PostgreSQL policy state store and PostgreSQL reconciliation store. Each request carries a distinct execution reference, so idempotency cannot collapse them and the nonce must do the work.

attack: Control — same 20-way race against the in-memory stores
expectation: Recorded to establish what the single-process race can and cannot demonstrate.
observed: 1 released, 1 settlement calls against the in-memory stores. The in-process race is won by the event loop rather than by the database, so a passing single-process result is not evidence of durable atomicity. The cross-process case supplies that evidence.

attack: Concurrent nonce race across 20 separate OS processes, each with its own connection pool
expectation: Exactly one process consumes the nonce; every other is refused. This is the case the reference paper exploited.
observed: 20 processes converged on one decision at a shared wall-clock instant: 1 consumed, 19 conflict, 0 other. Statuses: {"conflict:NONCE_ALREADY_CONSUMED":19,"consumed":1}. Reservation is a single INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING inside a transaction (postgres-store/src/store.ts:141), so exactly one transaction can return a row.
notes: Answers the question the F-2 redesign depends on: nonce reservation is already atomic at the database level, so F-2 does not require a store redesign — it requires the non-durable default to stop being the default.
